\chapter{Today, and How Much}
\label{ch:hi-today-and-how-much}
\hlchaptermodality{71}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can place a thing in today, add myself to it, raise it, and ask when and why when I ask after somebody.}

Complete HI-C71-why and say all five words in order, then say the six Hindi asking words as one family.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[āj]{\hi{आज} (āj) — today}

\label{lesson:HI-C71-today}



\begin{quote}
Two words back: what does \emph{gānā} mean, and what is \textbf{\hi{आराम}}? The next five words are the small ones that hold a conversation together.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{आज}}
\textbf{\hi{आज}} (\emph{āj}) — \textquotedblleft{}today\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \hi{अद्य} (\emph{adya}), \textquotedblleft{}today\textquotedblright{}, built from \textquotedblleft{}this\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}. Latin did exactly the same thing with \emph{hōc diē}, \textquotedblleft{}on this day\textquotedblright{}, which wore down to \emph{hodiē} and then to French \emph{aujourd'hui} and Spanish \emph{hoy}. Two families, the same idea, the same squeezing.

You already own \textbf{\hi{कल}} and \textbf{\hi{परसों}}, which reach forward and back. \hi{आज} is the missing middle of that set, and it is the one you will say most.

\textbf{\hi{आज} \hi{आप} \hi{कैसे} \hi{हैं}?} is the greeting you have been making, with one word added that makes it about now rather than in general.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five small words that do a great deal of work.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{gānā}, then read \textbf{\hi{आराम}} and say what it means
  \item \emph{Hear:} \emph{āj}, then \emph{kal}, then \emph{parsoṁ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{āj}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{āj āp kaise haiṁ?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{आज} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}today\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhī]{\hi{भी} (bhī) — also, too}

\label{lesson:HI-C71-also}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{āj}, then write \textbf{\hi{आज}}. Two letters, no matras: \hi{आ}, then \hi{ज}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{भी}}
\textbf{\hi{भी}} (\emph{bhī}) — \textquotedblleft{}also, too\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \hi{अपि} (\emph{api}), \textquotedblleft{}also\textquotedblright{}, is the ancestor. The Prakrits dropped the opening vowel and left a bare \emph{vi}; that hardened on the way into Hindi and came out as \hi{भी}. Two letters at the end of two thousand years, and the meaning has not moved at all.

The thing to hold on to is where it stands: \hi{भी} comes \textbf{after} the word it adds to, never before. \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{भी}} is \textquotedblleft{}me too\textquotedblright{}. \textbf{\hi{आज} \hi{भी}} is \textquotedblleft{}today as well\textquotedblright{}. Put it first and a Hindi ear hears nothing.

Watch out for one collision. You already own \textbf{\hi{अभी}}, \textquotedblleft{}right now\textquotedblright{}, and \hi{भी} is sitting inside it — but they are separate words with separate jobs, the way \textbf{\hi{अब}} and \textbf{\hi{अभी}} were. The eye will confuse them long before the ear does.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\hi{आज} and \hi{भी}, and a pair to keep apart.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\hi{आराम}}, then say it without looking
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{maiṁ bhī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{āj bhī}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{आज} once more, then \hi{भी} beside it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \hi{भी} stand, before or after the word it adds to? (After.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bahut]{\hi{बहुत} (bahut) — very, a lot}

\label{lesson:HI-C71-very}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}me too\textquotedblright{} in Hindi, and then \textquotedblleft{}today as well\textquotedblright{}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{बहुत}}
\textbf{\hi{बहुत}} (\emph{bahut}) — \textquotedblleft{}very, a lot, much\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \hi{बहु} (\emph{bahu}), \textquotedblleft{}much, many\textquotedblright{}. The same ancient root gave Greek \emph{pakhús}, \textquotedblleft{}thick\textquotedblright{}, so the family has always been about quantity of stuff.

\hi{बहुत} goes \textbf{before} what it strengthens, which is the opposite of \hi{भी}. You now have one small word that leans forward and one that leans back, and putting each on the wrong side is the commonest mistake a beginner makes with them.

Three you can say immediately, from words you already hold: \textbf{\hi{बहुत} \hi{बड़ा}}, \textbf{\hi{बहुत} \hi{धन्यवाद}}, \textbf{\hi{बहुत} \hi{जल्दी}}. That last one means \textquotedblleft{}very soon\textquotedblright{} as readily as \textquotedblleft{}very fast\textquotedblright{}, which is how \hi{बहुत} behaves throughout: it takes the colour of whatever it is standing in front of.

Set it against \textbf{\hi{कम}} and \textbf{\hi{ज़्यादा}}, which you learnt for measuring. \hi{बहुत} is not a comparison; it is an intensity.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: \hi{आज}, \hi{भी}, \hi{बहुत}. One that places the day, one that adds, one that raises.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bahut baṛā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bahut dhanyavād}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{bahut} before its word, and \emph{bhī} after its word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{बहुत} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}very\textquotedblright{}.) Say that something is very big.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kab]{\hi{कब} (kab) — when}

\label{lesson:HI-C71-when}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\hi{बहुत}} from memory: \hi{ब}, \hi{ह}, \hi{ु} underneath the \hi{ह}, then \hi{त}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{कब}}
\textbf{\hi{कब}} (\emph{kab}) — \textquotedblleft{}when\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \hi{कदा} (\emph{kadā}), \textquotedblleft{}when\textquotedblright{}. Look at the first letter and you have the whole point of this lesson: every Hindi asking word starts with \textbf{\hi{क}}.

You have been collecting them without being told they were a set: \emph{kyā}, \emph{kaun}, \emph{kahā̃}, \emph{kaise} — what, who, where, how — and now \textbf{\hi{कब}}, when. Five of them, every one written with a \hi{क} at the front, all doing the same job.

That letter is the signal. Hear a \textbf{\hi{क}} at the front of a short word at the head of somebody's sentence and you are being asked something, before you have worked out what.

\hi{कब} sits where the answer would sit, not at the front of the sentence the way an English question word does: \textbf{\hi{गाड़ी} \hi{कब} \hi{है}?}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and the fifth member of a family you already had.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kyā, kaun, kahā̃, kaise, kab}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gāṛī kab hai?}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{कब}, two letters and nothing else
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{कब} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}when\textquotedblright{}.) What letter do the asking words share?
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kyoṁ]{\hi{क्यों} (kyoṁ) — why, and \hi{क्योंकि}, because}

\label{lesson:HI-C71-why}



\begin{quote}
Name the four words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{क्यों}}
\textbf{\hi{क्यों}} (\emph{kyoṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}why\textquotedblright{}.

The sixth of the asking words, and it opens on the same \textbf{\hi{क}} as the other five. The spelling stacks \hi{क} on \hi{य} with the vowel-killer, then puts \hi{ों} on the end: the \hi{ो} matra and the dot that sends the vowel through the nose.

Now the piece that makes it useful twice over. Add \textbf{\hi{कि}} and you get \textbf{\hi{क्योंकि}} (\emph{kyoṁki}) — \textquotedblleft{}because\textquotedblright{}. \hi{कि} on its own is the little word that means \textquotedblleft{}that\textquotedblright{}, and \hi{क्योंकि} is literally \textquotedblleft{}why-that\textquotedblright{}: the question turned round to face the answer.

So one shape gives you both halves of a reason.

\textbf{\hi{आप} \hi{क्यों} \hi{नहीं} \hi{आए}?} asks it, and any answer that opens on \textbf{\hi{क्योंकि}} is giving the reason back. You will fill in what follows as your words grow.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \hi{आज}, \hi{भी}, \hi{बहुत}, \hi{कब}, \hi{क्यों}. Six asking words in all, and the way to answer the last of them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kyoṁ}, then \emph{kyoṁki}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kyā, kaun, kahā̃, kaise, kab, kyoṁ}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{कब}, then \hi{क्यों} beside the printed model
  \item \emph{Say it:} all five of this chapter in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{क्यों} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}why\textquotedblright{}.) And \hi{क्योंकि}? (\textquotedblleft{}because\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
